[2022 fall ms math-stat — problem 3]

Two COVID-19 vaccines (A, B) and a control: $n$ observations from group A, $m$ from B, $k$ from control. Overall mean $\mu$, group effects $\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \alpha_3$. (1) Write a regression model for the vaccination effects. (2) Give the corresponding model matrix. (3) Can all of $\mu, \alpha_1, \alpha_2, \alpha_3$ be estimated? If not, why, and give a fix.

response.text:
### (1) Regression model

Let the observations be ordered as

\[
Y_{A1},\dots,Y_{An},\quad Y_{B1},\dots,Y_{Bm},\quad Y_{C1},\dots,Y_{Ck},
\]

where \(C\) denotes the control group. A standard one-way ANOVA/regression model is

\[
Y_{ij}=\mu+\alpha_i+\varepsilon_{ij}, \qquad i=1,2,3,
\]

where

\[
i=1 \text{ for vaccine A},\qquad i=2 \text{ for vaccine B},\qquad i=3 \text{ for control},
\]

and typically

\[
\varepsilon_{ij}\stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim} N(0,\sigma^2)
\]

or at least are independent with mean \(0\) and common variance \(\sigma^2\). Thus the group means are

\[
\theta_1=\mu+\alpha_1,\qquad 
\theta_2=\mu+\alpha_2,\qquad 
\theta_3=\mu+\alpha_3.
\]

---

### (2) Model matrix

Let

\[
\beta=(\mu,\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\alpha_3)^\top.
\]

Then the model can be written as

\[
Y=X\beta+\varepsilon,
\]

where, with the observations ordered by group,

\[
X=
\begin{pmatrix}
\mathbf 1_n & \mathbf 1_n & \mathbf 0_n & \mathbf 0_n\\
\mathbf 1_m & \mathbf 0_m & \mathbf 1_m & \mathbf 0_m\\
\mathbf 1_k & \mathbf 0_k & \mathbf 0_k & \mathbf 1_k
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Equivalently, the rows are

\[
\begin{array}{c|cccc}
\text{group} & \mu & \alpha_1 & \alpha_2 & \alpha_3\\
\hline
A & 1 & 1 & 0 & 0\\
B & 1 & 0 & 1 & 0\\
C & 1 & 0 & 0 & 1
\end{array}
\]

repeated \(n,m,k\) times respectively.

---

### (3) Estimability of \(\mu,\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\alpha_3\)

No, the four parameters cannot all be estimated as written.

The reason is that the design matrix \(X\) is not full column rank. Its first column is the sum of the three group-indicator columns:

\[
\mathbf 1_{n+m+k}=z_1+z_2+z_3.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\operatorname{rank}(X)=3<4.
\]

Equivalently,

\[
X
\begin{pmatrix}
1\\
-1\\
-1\\
-1
\end{pmatrix}
=0,
\]

so the null space of \(X\) is nontrivial. For any constant \(c\),

\[
\mu'=\mu+c,\qquad \alpha_i'=\alpha_i-c,\quad i=1,2,3,
\]

gives exactly the same fitted values because

\[
\mu'+\alpha_i'=\mu+\alpha_i.
\]

Thus \(\mu,\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\alpha_3\) are not separately identifiable. Only combinations such as

\[
\mu+\alpha_i
\]

and contrasts such as

\[
\alpha_1-\alpha_3,\qquad \alpha_2-\alpha_3
\]

are estimable.

A common fix is to impose a constraint, for example

\[
\alpha_1+\alpha_2+\alpha_3=0.
\]

Then the parameters become identifiable. Under this constraint,

\[
\mu=\frac{\theta_1+\theta_2+\theta_3}{3},
\]

and the least-squares estimators are

\[
\widehat{\mu}
=
\frac{\bar Y_A+\bar Y_B+\bar Y_C}{3},
\]

\[
\widehat{\alpha}_1=\bar Y_A-\widehat{\mu},\qquad
\widehat{\alpha}_2=\bar Y_B-\widehat{\mu},\qquad
\widehat{\alpha}_3=\bar Y_C-\widehat{\mu}.
\]

If one wants \(\mu\) to be the sample-size weighted grand mean, then instead impose

\[
n\alpha_1+m\alpha_2+k\alpha_3=0,
\]

giving

\[
\widehat{\mu}
=
\frac{n\bar Y_A+m\bar Y_B+k\bar Y_C}{n+m+k}.
\]

Another common fix is to use the control group as the baseline by setting \(\alpha_3=0\). Then the model becomes

\[
Y_{ij}=\beta_0+\delta_1 I\{i=A\}+\delta_2 I\{i=B\}+\varepsilon_{ij},
\]

where

\[
\beta_0=\theta_3,\qquad
\delta_1=\theta_1-\theta_3,\qquad
\delta_2=\theta_2-\theta_3.
\]

The corresponding full-rank design matrix has rows

\[
\begin{array}{c|ccc}
\text{group} & \beta_0 & \delta_1 & \delta_2\\
\hline
A & 1 & 1 & 0\\
B & 1 & 0 & 1\\
C & 1 & 0 & 0
\end{array}
\]

and the vaccine effects relative to control are estimated by

\[
\widehat{\delta}_1=\bar Y_A-\bar Y_C,\qquad
\widehat{\delta}_2=\bar Y_B-\bar Y_C.
\]

So the original four-parameter model is overparameterized; one must impose a constraint or remove one redundant column.
